drivingQuestion: Does המוציא mean «who brought forth» (past), so that it is the proper wording of the blessing over bread?
outcomeNote: The unit closes with a halakhic decision: the blessing is המוציא לחם מן הארץ, following the Rabbis; the son of Rav Zevid's מוציא is defended only as a way of avoiding the dispute.

segments.he: וְרַבָּנַן? — הָהוּא הָכִי קָאָמַר לְהוּ קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל: כַּד מַפֵּיקְנָא לְכוּ, עָבֵידְנָא לְכוּ מִלְּתָא כִּי הֵיכִי דְּיָדְעִיתוּ דַּאֲנָא הוּא דְּאַפֵּיקִית יָתְכוֹן מִמִּצְרַיִם, דִּכְתִיב: ״וִידַעְתֶּם כִּי אֲנִי ה׳ אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הַמּוֹצִיא״.
segments.en: «And the Rabbis,» how do they respond to that proof? The Sages interpret «that» verse to mean that «the Holy one, Blessed be He, said to Israel as follows: When I bring you forth, I will perform something for you that you will know that I am the one who brought you forth from Egypt, as it is written: “And you will know that I am the Lord your God who brought you forth [hamotzi]”;» in this verse, too, hamotzi refers to the past.

segments.he: מִשְׁתַּבְּחִין לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן לְרַבִּי זֵירָא [אֶת] בַּר רַב זְבִיד אֲחוּהּ דְּרַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר רַב זְבִיד דְּאָדָם גָּדוֹל הוּא וּבָקִי בִּבְרָכוֹת הוּא. אָמַר לָהֶם: לִכְשֶׁיָּבֹא לְיֶדְכֶם הֲבִיאוּהוּ לְיָדִי. זִמְנָא חֲדָא אִיקְּלַע לְגַבֵּיהּ אַפִּיקוּ לֵיהּ רִיפְתָּא, פָּתַח וְאָמַר ״מוֹצִיא״. אָמַר: זֶה הוּא שֶׁאוֹמְרִים עָלָיו דְּאָדָם גָּדוֹל הוּא וּבָקִי בִּבְרָכוֹת הוּא?! בִּשְׁלָמָא אִי אֲמַר ״הַמּוֹצִיא״
segments.en: On that note, the Gemara relates: «The Sages would praise son of Rav Zevid, brother of Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Zevid to Rabbi Zeira, that he is a great man and he is expert in blessings.» Rabbi Zeira «said to» the Sages: «When he comes to you, bring him to me» so that I can meet him. «One day he happened» to come «before him. They brought out bread» to the guest, «he began and recited: Who brought forth [motzi] bread from the earth.» Rabbi Zeira grew annoyed «and said: This is he of whom they say that he is a great man and expert in blessings? Granted, had he recited: Hamotzi,»

segments.he: אַשְׁמְעִינַן טַעְמָא, וְאַשְׁמְעִינַן דְּהִלְכְתָא כְּרַבָּנַן. אֶלָּא דַּאֲמַר ״מוֹצִיא״ מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן? וְאִיהוּ דַּעֲבַד לְאַפּוֹקֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ מִפְּלוּגְתָּא.
segments.en: I would have understood that «he» thereby «taught us the meaning» of the verse: “Who brought you forth from Egypt,” «and he» thereby «taught us that the halakha is in accordance with» the opinion of «the Rabbis. However, what did he teach us by reciting motzi?» Everyone agrees that one fulfills his obligation when reciting motzi. The Gemara explains: The son of Rav Zevid «did this» in order «to preclude himself from» taking sides in «the dispute.» He preferred to phrase his blessing in a manner appropriate according to all opinions, rather than teach a novel concept, which is not universally accepted.

segments.he: וְהִלְכְתָא ״הַמּוֹצִיא לֶחֶם מִן הָאָרֶץ״, דְּקַיְימָא לַן כְּרַבָּנַן, דְּאָמְרִי דְּאַפֵּיק מַשְׁמַע.
segments.en: The Gemara concludes: «And the halakha» is that one recites: «Who brings forth [hamotzi] bread from the earth, as we hold in accordance with» the opinion of «the Rabbis who say» that it also means: Who brought forth.

moves.cueHe: ההוא הכי קאמר להו קודשא בריך הוא לישראל
moves.summary: On the Rabbis' behalf: the verse means that God told Israel that when He brings them out He will do something so that they will know He is the one who brought them out.
moves.about: the setama supplies the Rabbis' reading of the verse — God told Israel that when He brings them out He will do something so they will know He is the one who brought them out, so המוציא there too is past tense

moves.summary: The Gemara asks how the Rabbis account for the verse adduced in the preceding unit against their reading of המוציא.
moves.about: how the Rabbis account for the verse «וידעתם כי אני ה׳ אלהיכם המוציא», which was adduced against their view that המוציא denotes past action

moves.summary: The verse «וידעתם כי אני ה׳ אלהיכם המוציא» is quoted to show that its המוציא too is past tense.
moves.about: the verse's המוציא is read as past tense — the knowing is future, the bringing out is not

moves.summary: An anecdote is attached: the Sages praise the son of Rav Zevid to R' Zeira as a great man and expert in blessings.
moves.about: the Sages commend the son of Rav Zevid to R' Zeira as a great man and an expert in blessings

moves.cueHe: אמר להם: לכשיבא לידכם הביאוהו לידי
moves.summary: R' Zeira asks them to bring the man to him when he comes their way.
moves.about: R' Zeira asks the Sages to bring the man to him when he comes their way

moves.summary: He once comes before R' Zeira, bread is brought out, and he opens the blessing with «מוציא».
moves.about: the son of Rav Zevid once happened to come before R' Zeira and was served bread there

moves.cueHe: אמר: זה הוא שאומרים עליו דאדם גדול הוא ובקי בברכות הוא?!
moves.summary: R' Zeira protests that this is not the blessing of the man they praised as expert.
moves.about: whether a man reputed to be expert in blessings would open with מוציא rather than המוציא

moves.summary: Granted, had he said המוציא he would have taught the sense of the verse and that the halakha follows the Rabbis — but what does מוציא teach? (the move runs on into berakhot.38b.1)
moves.about: what the wording מוציא could possibly teach, since המוציא would have taught both the sense of the verse and that the halakha follows the Rabbis, whereas everyone agrees מוציא discharges the obligation

moves.summary: He acted so deliberately, to keep himself out of the dispute by blessing in wording valid on all views rather than teaching a contested novelty.
moves.about: why the son of Rav Zevid said מוציא although it teaches nothing — he wished to keep himself out of the dispute and bless in wording valid on every view

moves.summary: The halakha is to bless «המוציא לחם מן הארץ», since we hold like the Rabbis that the form connotes «who brought forth».
moves.about: which wording of the blessing over bread is the halakha — the sugya decides for המוציא לחם מן הארץ, following the Rabbis
